If that search fails too, no global ASID is handed out. The test for !global_asid_available is removed, because use_global_asid() only calls allocate_global_asid() if global_asid_available > 0. The remaining test is for a condition that should be impossible. [ riel: simplify code, massage changelog and comment ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommu/amd: Force device table to maximum size IOMMU can perform out-of-bounds read of the device table entry (DTE) that is adjacent to the last DTE and falls outside the device table. For example, if the device table can hold 0 to N-1 entries, then the IOMMU can be made to fetch the Nth entry, which falls outside the device table. The device table is owned by the hypervisor (HV) and is assigned in 4KB pages that are contiguous in system physical address (SPA). If the out-of-bound DTE falls on a guest-owned page, then the guest can exploit this bug to setup malicious table walks to corrupt HV pages and/or bring down the system. Note that this bug does not manifest when the device table size is set to its maximum size of 2MB. Therefore, force the device table size to the maximum 2MB on affected processors. These are CPU family 0x17 (Zen1/Zen2) through family 0x1a (Zen5/BRH). This is a mitigation for CVE-2024-21963. kdump reuses the previous kernel's device table only when the size encoded in the IOMMU device-table register matches pci_seg->dev_table_size. A mixed rollout disagrees: the unpatched kernel uses the IVRS-derived size and the patched kernel uses 2MB, so __reuse_device_table() rejects the table. On SNP-capable IOMMUs that rejection panics the kdump kernel. Kernels that both have this patch agree on 2MB and reuse succeeds. Update the production kernel and the crash kernel together.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ceph: clamp the inline data length in ceph_fill_inline_data() The MDS decides how much inline data to attach to a reply, and the client parses inline_len without any upper bound: ceph_decode_need() only verifies that the message actually carries that many bytes. ceph_fill_inline_data() then copies the data into a single folio with no length check, so a malicious or buggy MDS returning more inline data than the folio can hold writes past its end. Clamp the length to folio_size() so both callers, handle_cap_grant() and fill_inode(), are covered.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: batman-adv: tt: clear ROAM flag when re-adding a pending local client When a ROAMING_ADV is received for an announced local client, batadv_tt_local_mark_removed() sets BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM, queues a DEL|ROAM change and marks the entry as BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING. If the client sends a frame again before the next TTVN commit, batadv_tt_local_add_existing() only clears the PENDING flag and returns early. The ADD cancels the queued DEL, but the entry keeps the ROAM flag: * batadv_is_my_client() reports the client as not served by this node * batadv_tt_local_client_is_roaming() reroutes unicast frames for it to the node which sent the ROAMING_ADV The ROAM flag is only removed with the next frame of the client. Since BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM is set together with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING, it has to be cleared also at the same time with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING when the client roamed back.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: batman-adv: tt: only update flags for TT events In the first implementation of the translation table events, it was only possible to announce: * ADD: new locally detected client * DEL: disappeared local client If an ADD event was queued and then a DEL event was queued in the same timeslot, it is valid to destroy both events because nothing actually changed for remode nodes But with commit 3c4f7ab60cc2 ("batman-adv: improve the TT component to support runtime flag changes") and subsequent changes, it could also happen that there are extra ADD events: * ADD: _NEW_ locally detected client * ADD: already existing client with new flags * DEL: disappeared local client The first and the last type of event could in theory still be removed together from the (to be announced) events queue. But if the "update flags" ADD is dropped together with the DEL, it would still leave global translation table of a remote node in the incorrect state - believing that the client didn't disappear. If a detected client was previously announced, a DEL event must only overwrite the "update flags" ADD but the DEL itself must still continue to exist in the (to be anounced) events queue. For now, adjustment of the announced flags is used for everything instead of dropping already queued up events completely. Similarly, a DEL followed by an ADD caused both entries to be deleted. But the new ADD could announce flags changes which were not yet present for the client before it was marked for DELetion. The new ADD must therefore only overwrite the DEL - but still be kept.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ata: libata-scsi: reject data-in commands with a data-out buffer SG_IO can submit a data-in SCSI command with DMA_TO_DEVICE. The scatterlist can then contain pages pinned without write access. ata_scsi_rbuf_fill() writes simulated replies to that scatterlist; in the reported case, the copy tried to write the shared zero page and faulted in the kernel. The same mismatch can affect SG_IO commands translated by libata. ZBC IN and GET PHYSICAL ELEMENT STATUS completion handlers can modify the receive buffer even if the drive aborts the command. For ATAPI, the successful INQUIRY completion also rewrites the buffer in atapi_fixup_inquiry(). Reject these mismatched commands before the buffer is written or the command is issued. Report ABORTED COMMAND / DATA IN BUFFER ERROR because the CDB itself can be valid; the supplied transfer direction is wrong.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommu/arm-smmu-v3: Handle ARM erratum for CONT under invalidation with SVA The erratum (MMU-700: #3777127, S3: #3673557) deals with under invalidation of a CONT PTE grouping in the SMMU. The recommended work around is to use a range invalidation that spans the entire CONT. The only user of CONT in the kernel right now is through SVA sharing a CPU page table that contains a CONT created by the mm. Previously it was thought that this errata was dealt with because the driver always uses range invalidation. However, there is a subtle detail in the errata that the invalidation range must fully enclose the entire CONT for it to work. It seems that two sequential range invalidations, with a split point falling inside a CONT grouping, will not prevent the errata. The SMMU's range invalidation generation algorithm does not produce a single invalidation for a single SVA invalidation request, nor does the mm carefully align the SVA invalidation ranges to accommodate the splitting of the invalidation into several ranges. Thus, when processing a SVA invalidation, the range invalidation splitting routine can generate a range invalidation that is split in the middle of the CONT and risk under invalidation from this errata. This condition could be triggered by a malicious userspace manipulating the TLB gathers via mmap/mprotect/munmap. Update the errata list to the include the S3 variation, detect the IOMMUs that have it, and then have SVA invalidations use a simplified version of the over invalidation algorithm from the tlbi rework series. This ensures that a single range invalidation is issued for a single MMU notifier callback and now the range invalidation is guarenteed to cover any posible CONT. Future work to add CONT to iommu_domain page tables should either use this one-invalidate/one-range invalidation algorithm or disable CONT support in the iommu_domain.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: arm64: Use kvm_s2_fault_vma_info in gmem_abort() gmem_abort() maps at s2fd->fault_ipa, which HPFAR_EL2 holds at 4K granularity whatever the page size. The generic page-table code aligns it, but pkvm_pgtable_stage2_map() looks up existing mappings over [addr, addr + size), so on a pKVM host with pages larger than 4K a guest_memfd-backed guest that faults past the first 4K of a page can find its neighbour's mapping, get -EAGAIN and take the same fault forever. The memory fault exit reports s2fd->fault_ipa too, which for a nested guest's fault is the nested IPA rather than the canonical one kvm_gmem_get_pfn() failed on. Take the addresses from kvm_s2_fault_vma_info instead, as user_mem_abort() does, and report the canonical gfn in the memory fault exit. kvm_s2_fault_get_vma_info() itself isn't called: a guest_memfd memslot's userspace_addr doesn't need to be backed by a VMA.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to avoid folio->mapping dereference in is_{meta, node}_folio() Otherwise, it may cause NULL pointer dereference in race condition: Thread A Thread B - f2fs_setattr - f2fs_truncate - f2fs_truncate_blocks - f2fs_do_truncate_blocks - f2fs_truncate_inode_blocks - truncate_dnode - truncate_node - invalidate_mapping_pages - folio->mapping = NULL - folio_lock - is_node_folio - F2FS_F_SB(folio): dereference on folio->mapping

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: sctp: hold shkey across socket migration sctp_sock_migrate() transfers queued DATA skbs from the old socket to the new one. skb_orphan() invokes sctp_wfree() during that transfer and drops the skb-owned shared-key reference. If userspace has removed that key from the association, this can be the final reference. The following sctp_set_owner_w() then dereferences the freed chunk->shkey while trying to take the new owner reference. Take a temporary shared-key reference before orphaning the skb and release it after the new owner has taken its reference. This preserves the selected authentication key throughout the ownership transfer. Bug found and triaged by OpenAI Security Research and validated by Trail of Bits.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: sctp: re-point retained control chunks on association migration sctp_sock_migrate() transfers DATA chunk ownership but leaves retained control chunks pointing at the old socket. A later retransmission can therefore access the socket after it has been freed. Extend the migration walk to cover retained control chunks and use sctp_control_set_owner_w() to assign their new owner. Reuse the DATA ownership check so each chunk is processed once per pass, even when it is reachable through multiple lists or retained pointers. Preserve a control chunk's existing authentication key across migration so its final release can still generate SCTP_AUTH_FREE_KEY when needed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: platform/chrome: cros_usbpd_notify: Only use drvdata when parent is GOOG0004 cros_usbpd_notify_probe_acpi() takes the EC device pointer from dev_get_drvdata(dev->parent) and assumes it is a struct cros_ec_device. That only holds when GOOG0003 is a child of GOOG0004. On older devices without that hierarchy, such as Google Nami, GOOG0003 and GOOG0004 are siblings under the ACPI EC (PNP0C09): PNP0C09:00 (acpi-ec) |-- GOOG0003:00 (cros-usbpd-notify-acpi) `-- GOOG0004:00 (cros_ec_lpcs) Before commit db65a06d10b3 ("ACPI: EC: Convert the driver to a platform one") the parent platform device had no driver data, so the driver warned and continued without an EC pointer, as intended for these devices. Since that commit the ACPI EC driver stores its struct acpi_ec there, so the driver treats a struct acpi_ec as a struct cros_ec_device and calls cros_ec_cmd() on it for every USB-C PD host event. Plugging or unplugging a charger then intermittently oopses, followed by soft lockups and a hung system: BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffff9cf03220 #PF: supervisor write access in kernel mode Hardware name: Google Nami/Nami, BIOS 09/19/2019 Workqueue: kacpi_notify acpi_os_execute_deferred RIP: 0010:native_queued_spin_lock_slowpath+0x29d/0x330 Call Trace: _raw_spin_lock_irqsave+0x59/0x80 __mutex_lock.constprop.0+0x129/0x930 cros_ec_cmd_xfer+0x2a/0xf0 [cros_ec_proto] cros_ec_cmd_xfer_status+0x1a/0x90 [cros_ec_proto] cros_ec_cmd+0xb7/0x140 [cros_ec_proto] cros_usbpd_get_event_and_notify+0x42/0xc0 [cros_usbpd_notify] acpi_ev_notify_dispatch+0x4e/0x70 acpi_os_execute_deferred+0x1a/0x30 Only read the parent's driver data when the parent's ACPI node is GOOG0004, and otherwise continue without an EC pointer. While at it, drop the reference taken by fwnode_get_parent().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings find_vma_and_prepare_anon() can end up allocating an anon_vma in VMAs that are not CoW mappings, which is wrong. If we have a MAP_SHARED R/O file mapped, we lack VM_SHARED (but do have VM_MAYSHARE) and lack VM_MAYWRITE. While uffd later rejects such mappings (uffd registration requires VM_MAYWRITE, see comment in validate_dst_vma) find_vma_and_prepare_anon() still wrongly allocates an anon vma before it validates the vma. This in turn later confuses copy_page_range()->vma_needs_copy() such that we end up calling copy_hugetlb_page_range() with ranges that actually do not contain *any* per-pagetable information that would require copying, which is the basis for PMD-table sharing in the first place. copy_hugetlb_page_range() should not have to worry about shared PMD tables at all: it doesn't make any sense to copy page tables that are shared, as they can be fully recreated later. Ending up in the function with shareable page tables is the real issue. If a destination PMD table is shared in copy_hugetlb_page_range(), it might get concurrently unshared as we are not holding relevant locks, resulting in us using a page table that is no longer mapped and possibly freed after calling: dst_pte = huge_pte_alloc(dst, dst_vma, addr, sz); To fix it, do not allocate an anon_vma in non-CoW mappings and add a safety guard to copy_hugetlb_page_range(), making sure that we never end up messing with shared PMD tables in there. Before commit 867a43a34ff8a ("userfaultfd: use per-vma locks in userfaultfd operations") we would always validate the VMA before allocating an anon_vma, and consequently never wrongly allocate an anon_vma. As uffd_lock_vma() is part of the same lookup machinery and also contains a misleading VM_SHARED check, change that one as well directly for consistency. A follow-up cleanup will stop taking the hugetlb_vma_lock_read(src_vma) lock in copy_hugetlb_page_range() entirely. Further, the usage of VM_SHARED in userfaultfd code should be cleaned up later to focus on CoW vs. non-CoW mappings.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/shmem: honour F_SEAL_EXEC when an ACL is set The owner of a memfd sealed with F_SEAL_EXEC can still change its execute bits by setting a POSIX access ACL. With CONFIG_TMPFS_POSIX_ACL, this lets an unprivileged owner make a non-executable memfd executable, bypassing vm.memfd_noexec=2. simple_set_acl() updates i_mode directly, bypassing the seal check in shmem_setattr(). Add shmem_set_acl() to check the resulting mode. Share the F_SEAL_EXEC check with shmem_setattr() using memfd_check_seals_mode() in include/linux/memfd.h. Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private. [ david: use common helper; simplify description ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery In AP mode every broadcast and multicast data frame is routed to TX_DESC_QSEL_HIGH, the after-DTIM queue, whether or not anybody is asleep. The firmware drains that queue at beacon pace, a dozen or so frames per second measured on RTL8822BU, while one associated client's mDNS/SSDP chatter alone exceeds that. The excess accumulates inside the chip until the shared TX page pool is exhausted (measured: 14 of 1803 pages left). From that point every host-sourced frame queues behind the backlog: authentication responses reach the air seconds after the client has given up, so no station can associate anymore, and the beacon reserved-page download fails the BCN_VALID poll ("error beacon valid") because it needs pages from the same pool. The AP keeps beaconing, so the failure looks like a silent RX stall and only a reboot recovers. mac80211 already decides when after-DTIM delivery is needed: it sets IEEE80211_TX_CTL_SEND_AFTER_DTIM on bmc frames only while at least one station is actually dozing. Honor that instead of routing unconditionally: flagged frames keep going through the high queue with the MORE_DATA and HGQMD handling introduced by commit 076f786a0ae1 ("wifi: rtw88: Fix AP mode incorrect DTIM behavior"), everything else leaves at line rate through the AC queues. This partially reverts the usb.c hunk of that commit, whose unconditional routing is what lets the backlog build up. On a bench AP (USB2, 20 MHz, WPA2, hostapd, a Windows client driven through disconnect/reconnect cycles): reconnects fail 0/5 on RTL8822BU and 0/3 on RTL8821CU before this change, and pass 10/10 and 5/5 with it, with the page pool staying healthy and no beacon errors logged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: rtw88: usb: bound what the driver feeds the after-DTIM queue Frames routed to the high queue are transmitted right after DTIM beacons only, inside the ATIM window, while they wait in the shared TX page pool. The driver puts no limit on how many it hands over, so as long as one station dozes, any sustained broadcast or multicast traffic outruns the drain and empties the pool: measured on an RTL8822BU AP with a single client in power save and ~40 frames/s of mDNS chatter, the free page count at 0x240 goes from 1803 to 16 in about 100 seconds and stays there for as long as the traffic lasts. From that point every other transmit queues behind the backlog, authentication responses arrive too late for anyone to join, and the reserved page download fails ("error beacon valid"). The AP keeps beaconing and only a reboot recovers. Feed the high queue through a small budget that refills below the measured drain rate (about 3 frames per DTIM, ~15/s at dtim_period 2 on the default 2 TU ATIM window); whatever exceeds the budget leaves on its access category queue right away. The high queue backlog is now bounded by the burst size under any load, so the page pool cannot run dry, at the price that a dozing station may miss part of a broadcast storm.

This limit is set by the device driver/DMA controller (max_hw_sectors) and device-mapper targets. When flushing dirty pages (governed by VFS writeback_chunk_size() and f2fs nr_pages_to_skip()), f2fs merges contiguous pages into bios up to 512KB (1024 sectors) or more without checking queue_max_sectors, which will be split if the device or DM target enforces a smaller limit. 2. queue_max_segments: Splits bios exceeding scatter-gather segment limits. f2fs allocates bios with up to 256 pages, exceeding the 128-segment limit of DM targets (dm-default-key/dm-crypt) if pages are discontiguous. 3. chunk_sectors: Splits bios crossing chunk/zone boundaries. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: return -EIO for a lost inode block after cp_error After cp_error, dirty node caches are dropped without being written. If such an inode was never written, its NAT entry is still NEW_ADDR, and reading its inode block returns -ENOENT. f2fs_get_dnode_of_data() passes that -ENOENT up, and callers take it as a hole. Since the inode block is missing, the next offset can only advance one block, so fiemap walks block by block up to maxbytes, about 2^30 blocks, while holding the inode lock. It took hours in a power-off recovery test after shutdown and blocked unlink and umount on the file. Return -EIO instead of -ENOENT when the inode block itself is missing after cp_error or shutdown. A missing direct or indirect node is still reported as -ENOENT.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack sit_ver_bitmap_bytesize and nat_ver_bitmap_bytesize are used as memcpy lengths into and out of sbi->ckpt, which is sized from cp_payload alone, and nothing compares either length against that allocation. sanity_check_ckpt() has checked these two fields since c77ec61ca0a4, which added them after a crafted image overran build_sit_info(). That check ties each length to a segment count; it never compares either against the allocation, which is the half this adds. Mounting over-reads in build_sit_info() and build_node_manager(), and the first checkpoint writes the same lengths back through the same pointers, so the over-read's contents reach the on-disk checkpoint. An unmount is enough; the filesystem does not have to be used. Bound both ends the way __bitmap_ptr() lays them out. The three branches differ, so a single sum of the two lengths would still admit a small overflow when cp_payload is non-zero.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: arm64: vgic: Stop the target vcpu when disabling LPIs Disabling LPIs is pretty nasty, as it directly messes with the AP list of the affected CPU, which could be running... This has the potential to lead to really bad behaviours, and we should not be doing that. Take example on the way the Active state is handled and simply pause the the vcpu so that we are sure it is in a quiescent state, and the state be safely manipulated. Nobody has any expectation of performance for this anyway.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to avoid potential reference count leak in do_garbage_collect() In do_garbage_collect(), we have reserved reference counts on summary cache of all segments, once gc_thread encounter freezing, we need to release all reference counts.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvme-tcp: Validate the queue state under the queue lock in the address attribute Reading the "address" sysfs attribute calls kernel_getsockname() on the admin queue socket, which can race with the queue teardown during connection error recovery: a reader can observe NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE set, then block on the queue lock while nvme_tcp_free_queue() releases the socket and clears queue->sock without holding the lock. Once the reader acquires the lock it dereferences the NULL socket pointer. Commit 76d54bf20cdc ("nvme-tcp: don't access released socket during error recovery") had the queue liveness check inside the lock. Commit 782373ba2766 ("nvme: tcp: avoid race between queue_lock lock and destroy") moved it back out because the lock itself is destroyed in nvme_tcp_free_queue(), so a reader arriving late trips mutex_destroy(). Check the queue liveness inside the queue lock, and clear queue->sock under the same lock. The teardown clears NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE under the lock well before the socket is released, so a reader either sees the bit cleared or a socket that cannot be released while it holds the lock. To also close the lock lifetime race, the queue locks are now owned by the controller: they are initialized with the queue array and only destroyed when the controller is freed, which cannot happen while a sysfs attribute read is still in progress. The queue count is computed by the NVME_TCP_OPT_NR_QUEUES() macro from the original connect options for both initialization and destruction, as reconnects may shrink ctrl->queue_count.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to invalidate curseg if change_curseg() fails Our consistency stress test (fsstress + fio + atomic write workers + "f2fs_io shutdown 1") triggers below kernel BUG: F2FS-fs (vdd): Stopped filesystem due to reason: 0 ------------[ cut here ]------------ kernel BUG at fs/f2fs/segment.c:3989! Oops: invalid opcode: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI Workqueue: writeback wb_workfn (flush-253:48) RIP: 0010:f2fs_allocate_data_block+0x257a/0x38e0 Call Trace: <TASK> do_write_block+0x155/0xc10 f2fs_outplace_write_data+0x192/0x340 f2fs_do_write_data_page+0xc57/0x1880 f2fs_write_single_data_page+0xda9/0x15a0 f2fs_write_cache_pages+0x973/0x1f20 __f2fs_write_data_pages+0x6c4/0x1890 do_writepages+0x21e/0x560 __writeback_single_inode+0x119/0x11b0 writeback_sb_inodes+0x67d/0x17a0 wb_writeback+0x207/0x820 wb_workfn+0x128/0xc30 process_one_work+0x925/0x1600 worker_thread+0x60a/0xff0 kthread+0x35f/0x460 ret_from_fork+0x474/0x7e0 ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30 </TASK> The BUG is f2fs_bug_on(sbi, curseg->next_blkoff >= BLKS_PER_SEG(sbi)) in f2fs_allocate_data_block(), next_blkoff was 512. The root cause is a race in between atomic write commit and shutdown as below: Thread A (commit atomic write) Thread B (shutdown) Thread C (writeback) - f2fs_ioc_commit_atomic_write - f2fs_commit_atomic_write - __f2fs_commit_atomic_write - __replace_atomic_write_block - f2fs_replace_block - __f2fs_replace_block - f2fs_ioc_shutdown - f2fs_do_shutdown : F2FS_GOING_DOWN_METASYNC - f2fs_sync_fs - f2fs_write_single_data_page : pass f2fs_cp_error() check - f2fs_stop_checkpoint : set CP_ERROR_FLAG - change_curseg - reset_curseg : curseg->segno = new_segno : curseg->alloc_type = SSR : curseg->next_blkoff = __next_free_blkoff() which is BLKS_PER_SEG if there is no free slot in new_segno - f2fs_get_sum_cache : return -EIO due to f2fs_cp_error() : return error w/o restoring curseg : goto out_unlock, skip restoring old segno, blkoff and alloc_type - f2fs_do_write_data_page - f2fs_outplace_write_data - do_write_block - f2fs_allocate_data_block : curseg->segno is valid : f2fs_bug_on(next_blkoff >= BLKS_PER_SEG) Since commit 86f33603f8c5 ("f2fs: handle errors of f2fs_get_meta_page_nofail"), change_curseg() can fail after the curseg has already been switched to the new segment, then the curseg is left in an inconsistent state: it points to a segment which may have no free slot, its summary block is zeroed, and the caller can not restore it. Subsequent block allocation on the curseg will trigger the BUG. Moreover, the writeback thread dies with curseg_lock, curseg_mutex and sentry_lock held, so the commit, shutdown and other I/O threads hang in D state. Since change_curseg() only fails once CP_ERROR_FLAG is set, no checkpoint will be committed afterward, let's invalidate the curseg via reset_curseg_fields() on failure, as new_curseg() does for -ENOSPC, then f2fs_allocate_data_block() will fail with -ENOSPC on the curseg instead of triggering BUG, and do_write_block() can handle the error since CP_ERROR_FLA ---truncated---

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: release a removed xattr node in roll-forward recovery When xattrs shrink enough to fit in the inline xattr area, write_all_xattrs() truncates the xattr node and clears i_xattr_nid. If the file is then fsynced without a checkpoint, only the inode block is written, with i_xattr_nid of 0. Roll-forward recovery starts from the checkpointed inode, whose i_xattr_nid still points to the old xattr node. f2fs_recover_inline_xattr() copies only the inline xattr area, and f2fs_update_inode() writes the old i_xattr_nid back. So the inode keeps the stale xattr node: - The node block is never released, and fsck reports "nonzero bytes in xattr space after end of list". - If the inline xattr list ends exactly at the end of the inline area, its terminator is read from the stale node, and the removed xattrs come back after recovery. When the fsynced inode has no xattr node but the checkpointed one has, release the old xattr node as truncate_node() does: check its block address, invalidate the block and drop its node cache, which may still be dirty.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommufd/iova_bitmap: Ensure that iova_bitmap_set() handles the full IOVA Generally userspace is going to step the dirty bitmap through the IOVA space. However if the bitmap ends in the middle of a large PTE this is problematic. The first step will clear the dirty bit and report dirty to the end of its bitmap while the second step will see the clear'd dirty and report clean for the start of the bitmap. If it happens this ends up losing dirties. Further this function is missing bounds checking so if this does happen ther is a good chance it will write memory beyond what the userspace was expecting. Return an error code if this illegal condition happens.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one When a full node's leaves and the new key all share the node's segment, assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node() replaces the node with a shortcut to a pair of new nodes. If the node is itself the target of a shortcut, the new shortcut is installed as that shortcut's next node, and a shortcut leading to a shortcut is something nothing expects: assoc_array_walk() indexes the second one as a node, and assoc_array_apply_edit() hits the BUG_ON() in the loop that adjusts nr_leaves_on_branch, on that same insertion. Deletion gets a node there. When the subtree below a shortcut shrinks enough, assoc_array_delete() collapses it into one node below the shortcut, and the leaves it collects can all share that node's segment. The next key that shares it too takes this path. Eighteen insertions and a deletion are enough: sixteen keys that agree on bits 0-11, one that leaves them at bit 8 and is deleted again, and one more that agrees with the sixteen. Have the new shortcut replace the one in front of the node as well. assoc_array_insert_shortcut() gives it that shortcut's back pointer and parent slot, so the caller installs it where that one was, and excises the old shortcut along with the node, which takes a second entry in excised_meta[]. The new shortcut's index key comes from the new key up to the new skip level, so it covers what the old one did. Found by a userspace test doing random insertions and deletions on keys that share long prefixes; a targeted case builds a shortcut, deletes down to the collapse and inserts one more key.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree on allocation failure assoc_array_gc() builds a copy of the tree. Where the copy reaches a shortcut, it allocates the copy of the shortcut with kmalloc_flex(), fills it with memcpy(), links it into the new tree, and only then allocates the copy of the node after it. The memcpy() leaves the new shortcut's next_node pointing at the old tree's node, so if that second allocation fails, the cleanup, assoc_array_destroy_subtree() on the new tree, follows the new shortcut into the old tree, and the BUG_ON() on the old node's back pointer fires. Allocate the node first, and the shortcut once the node exists, freeing the node again if the shortcut cannot be allocated. A copied shortcut is then only linked into the new tree when the copy of its node is there to follow it. Nothing else changes: with no allocation failing, the trees gc builds are the same as before. Found by a userspace test that makes each allocation of each operation fail in turn.

Performing a manipulation results in allocation of resources. The attack can be initiated remotely. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.

A vulnerability was detected in smartalock wireguard-lwip up to cfba91666590e86bd67842c71cedf9a423be823a. This affects the function wireguard_generate_unique_index of the file src/wireguard.c of the component Session Index Allocator. The manipulation of the argument receiver_index results in allocation of resources. The attack is only possible with local access. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When a client application enforces step-up authentication or multi-factor authentication (MFA) via a minimum authentication level, Keycloak fails to apply this requirement to login sessions initiated through the credential reset endpoint. An attacker who possesses a user's initial credentials (such as a password) can navigate from the reset interface back to the standard login form and authenticate without completing the required second factor. This flaw allows an attacker to obtain valid access tokens and gain unauthorized access to protected services without satisfying mandatory security controls.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. The Account API endpoint for sharing resources fails to verify whether owner-managed access is enabled and accepts permission scopes not assigned to the resource. An authenticated user can exploit this vulnerability to generate pre-granted permission tickets, causing Keycloak to bypass policy evaluation and issue access tokens with unauthorized scopes.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When processing token requests using the User-Managed Access (UMA) grant, Keycloak fails to verify whether a target client or resource server is enabled before issuing an authorization token. An authenticated remote user can exploit this flaw to obtain valid Requesting Party Tokens (RPTs) for disabled clients, bypassing administrative access controls and permissions restrictions.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When an administrator revokes tokens by setting a not-before revocation cutoff, Keycloak fails to enforce this boundary when processing User-Managed Access (UMA) grant requests using ID token claims. An authenticated remote user with an active session can submit a previously revoked ID token to receive a fresh Requesting Party Token (RPT). This flaw allows an attacker to bypass token revocation and retain unauthorized access to protected resources.

An uncontrolled recursion vulnerability exists in the LINE iOS app prior to version 26.19.0. The Flex Message processing component does not adequately validate the structure of externally supplied message content. As a result, an attacker who is able to send a crafted message to a victim could cause the application to crash when the message is received or displayed. A server-side mitigation has been deployed that also protects existing iOS clients that have not been updated to version 26.19.0.

The Canva Desktop App before 1.128.0 stores encrypted application state on disk. The encryption key is hardcoded as a plaintext string in the main.js file and is identical across all Canva installations on Windows and macOS.

BeamNG.drive before 0.40.6 contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability because JIT-compiled LuaJIT traces omit FFI array bounds checks, letting untrusted Lua escape the sandbox. Attackers supplying a malicious mod can JIT-compile an FFI store loop, write out of range using a tostring() address leak, re-enable ffi.load, and run commands as the game user.

Bar Assistant 3.0.0 before 6.11.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in BarController::join that allows authenticated users to join bars without a valid invite code. Attackers can send POST requests to /api/bars/join omitting invite_code, matching invite-disabled bars with NULL codes, to read cocktails, ingredients, members, settings and search tokens.

Dokploy 0.28.0 before 0.31.1 contains a path traversal vulnerability in the patch.readRepoDirectories tRPC procedure that allows authenticated organization members to list tracked files of arbitrary git repositories. Attackers with service read permission can supply a crafted repoPath, which is passed to git ls-tree unconfined, to enumerate other organizations' application and compose source trees.

FFmpeg 7.0 through 9.0.2 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in dvdvideo_menu_next_ps_block() in libavformat/dvdvideodec.c when demuxing DVD menu domains. Attackers can craft a DVD image whose last cell sector and NAV next-VOBU pointer bypass the end-of-cell check, overreading pgc->cell_playback and crashing the process.

A vulnerability was determined in aoiflux mutant 2.3.0/2.4.0/2.5.0. This vulnerability affects unknown code of the file builtin/hive_builtins.go of the component Forensic Parser. This manipulation of the argument Count causes uncontrolled memory allocation. It is possible to launch the attack on the local host. Upgrading to version 2.6.0 is able to resolve this issue. Patch name: c4b1a7dec6c603115e2a05d1e8970a142f0b9774. Upgrading the affected component is recommended.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unbounded arc length in OBJECT IDENTIFIER decoding and encoding. The content of an OBJECT IDENTIFIER or RELATIVE-OID element is passed to unpack "w*" on decode, and the arcs of an OID string to pack "w*" on encode. Perl converts each arc to or from its decimal string in time quadratic in the arc's length, and nothing limits that length. An attacker who controls the decoded data, or an OID string passed to encode, can exhaust CPU with a single oversized arc.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via a declared element length passed unchecked to sysread in asn_read and asn_get. The length an element declares in its BER header is passed to sysread as the read size. Perl grows the target buffer to that size before reading, so memory is allocated from the declared length, not from the data received. A 6-byte header can declare a length of up to 4GB. A single header makes the reading process allocate the declared size. Where the allocation fails, perl exits with "Out of memory", which eval cannot catch.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unlimited recursion depth in constructed-form string decoding. Any constructed-form string element causes the decoder to recurse on the element's contents. The BER encoding controls nesting depth at four bytes per level, with no bound checked. Perl recursion is heap-allocated, so the process grows without a stack crash. An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a small deeply nested constructed string.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via zero-length BIT STRING content. A BIT STRING with zero content octets passes -1 to substr as the length. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the decoded value is nearly all of the input that follows the element. In the constructed form each zero-length segment copies the rest of the input again, so memory grows with the square of the input size. An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a short constructed BIT STRING. The resulting value also contains bytes from adjacent input.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via exponent-notation string in INTEGER encoding. The encoder routes any value with abs >= 2**31 to i2osp without validating that it is an integer. A string in exponent notation such as "1e8000" passes that threshold. Math::BigInt expands it to an 8001-digit integer, and i2osp's per-octet conversion loop is quadratic in that size. An attacker who controls encoded INTEGER values can exhaust CPU with a short exponent-notation string.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unchecked exponent length in binary REAL decoding. Binary REAL decoding never bounds-checks the exponent length against the available content. For a minimal one-byte binary REAL, the exponent byte is read from outside the element, making the mantissa length -1. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the mantissa is nearly all of the input that follows the element. The long-form exponent path also omits the extra length octet when sizing the mantissa. An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust CPU with a list of such values, as each mantissa loop iterates over the remaining input. The decoded values are also computed from bytes outside each element.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded MSG_PEEK buffer doubling in asn_recv. asn_recv peeks the socket in a loop, doubling the buffer size on each pass until a tag and length can be decoded. An inverted boolean guard ($tb || rather than $tb &&) prevents the need-more-data exit from firing once a tag byte has been decoded. When asn_decode_length returns no value because the length is absent or incomplete, no exit fires for that case either. MSG_PEEK leaves socket data unconsumed, so each re-peek returns at once while the buffer size doubles. A single truncated BER header sent to a process calling asn_recv doubles the peek buffer until memory is exhausted. Perl's realloc failure is fatal and not catchable with eval.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic bigint loop in os2ip. Every INTEGER or ENUMERATED longer than four content octets reaches os2ip, which iterates over each content octet with $result = ($result * 256) + $octet. Each multiplication operates on a bigint that grows by one octet per step, so decoding an n-octet value takes O(n^2) bigint work. Nothing limits content length before this loop runs. An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust CPU with a single oversized INTEGER or ENUMERATED value.

lwext4 through 1.0.0 contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in ext4_fs_init_block_bitmap() that allows attackers to corrupt heap memory via crafted superblock geometry fields. Attackers can supply an ext4 image with oversized s_reserved_gdt_blocks and BLOCK_UNINIT groups to write past the bitmap buffer, crashing applications that mount it.

lwext4 through 1.0.0 contains a heap buffer overflow in ext4_fs_init_inode_bitmap() in src/ext4_fs.c because it does not validate s_inodes_per_group against the inode bitmap size. Attackers can supply a crafted ext4 image with an oversized s_inodes_per_group so memset writes past the heap buffer, corrupting memory and crashing the mounting application.

StorageGRID (formerly StorageGRID Webscale) versions 12.1.0 and higher are susceptible to an information exposure vulnerability which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to acquire low-sensitivity credentials via a Man-in-the-middle attack when certain non-default features are enabled.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When configured with a database that uses case-insensitive collation, Keycloak resolves realm URLs regardless of letter casing. A remote attacker can exploit this behavior by sending requests with alternate letter casing to bypass upstream reverse proxy access controls that rely on case-sensitive path matching. This issue can expose restricted authentication endpoints intended only for internal access, though Keycloak's internal authentication mechanisms remain intact.

A vulnerability was identified in Dolibarr ERP CRM up to 23.0.4. This affects the function dol_convert_file in the library htdocs/core/lib/files.lib.php of the component Document Upload. Such manipulation leads to code injection. The attack can be launched remotely. The exploit is publicly available and might be used. Upgrading to version 24.0.0 is able to mitigate this issue. The name of the patch is 9b6368b2a9eae3eec690b2ce22c4f291f0051540. Upgrading the affected component is advised.

Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection') vulnerability in PublishPress PublishPress Authors publishpress-authors allows Blind SQL Injection.This issue affects PublishPress Authors: from n/a through 4.18.0.

Reliance on obfuscation or encryption of Security-Relevant inputs without integrity checking, Improper validation of integrity check value, Cleartext transmission of sensitive information vulnerability in the EncryptInterceptor of Apache Tomcat. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.13 through 9.0.123. The following versions were EOL at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: from 8.5.38 through 8.5.100, from 7.0.100 through 7.0.109. Other unsupported versions may also be affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.1.62 or 9.0.124 and switch to TLS-PSK to encrypt cluster communication, which fixes the issue. Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released

Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, validate_url_ssrf() in src/core/utils.py validates one DNS answer and then returns the hostname, while guarded_aiohttp_request(), enforce_outbound_url(), and validate_url_with_env_config() allow the outbound connection to perform an independent second lookup. A caller with control of the hostname's DNS can make validation see a public address and make the connection see an internal address, bypassing the guard across its outbound consumers and exposing readable internal or metadata-service responses. The attack requires low or zero DNS TTL behavior and a successful timing-dependent answer change; static multiple-address answers are checked and do not provide the same bypass. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, http.paginate in src/core/modules/atomic/http/paginate.py validates only the initial base_url, and _paginate_link_header then follows a server-supplied Link: rel="next" URL without calling the SSRF guard again. A low-privileged caller can make an allowed first page point the next request at an internal or metadata service, causing a readable second-order SSRF whose response body is aggregated into all_items and returned. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, the MCP run_recipe tool in src/core/mcp_handler.py accepts a caller-controlled recipe_name that load_recipe() in src/cli/recipe.py appends to the src/recipes path without resolved-path containment. Parent-directory segments can therefore make Flyto load and execute a YAML workflow outside the bundled recipe directory, bypassing the boundary represented by list_recipes(). This does not necessarily provide unrestricted code execution because available workflow modules remain subject to Flyto's module policy, but it permits unintended execution of allowed browser, network, file, and data-processing modules. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, validate_url_ssrf in src/core/utils.py resolves and checks a hostname but returns the hostname URL rather than the validated address, and session.get in http.get performs an independent DNS lookup when connecting. A low-privileged caller with control of the hostname's DNS can make the first lookup return a public address and the connection-time lookup return an internal address, bypassing the SSRF guard for all modules that call it and exposing readable internal or metadata-service responses. Successful exploitation requires attacker-controlled DNS and a successful timing-dependent answer change between the two lookups. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, the earlier CVE-2026-67429 remediation applied validate_path_with_env_config() to only a hand-picked set of file-writing modules, leaving data.csv.write in src/core/modules/atomic/data/csv_write.py, data.json_to_csv in src/core/modules/atomic/data/json_to_csv.py, file.copy in src/core/modules/atomic/file/copy.py, and file.move in src/core/modules/atomic/file/move.py outside the FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR confinement boundary. The advisory also identifies unguarded modules across the broader data.*, file.*, and report-writer families. data.csv.write relies on a .. substring denylist that does not reject absolute paths, while the other named modules accept caller-controlled output or destination paths without the canonical guard. A caller able to execute modules or recipes can therefore write attacker-controlled content outside the configured sandbox, potentially overwriting application code, recipes, startup files, scheduled-task files, or authorization files and gaining code execution on the host. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. From 0.0.20.Final until 0.0.27.Final, OHttpClientCodec in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpClientCodec.java and OHttpServerCodec in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpServerCodec.java retain the consumed outer cumulationBuffer after a valid OHTTP exchange completes, even though OHttpRequestResponseContext.destroy in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpRequestResponseContext.java releases the inner Binary HTTP cumulation and the channel remains active. A peer can complete a large request or response and leave the keep-alive connection idle, causing the client and server handlers to retain the current high-water pooled or direct buffer capacity until later inbound content replaces it or the handler is removed. Many long-lived idle connections can pin substantial memory and create availability pressure. The issue does not cause unbounded growth for repeated exchanges on a single channel. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.27.Final.

netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser.readFieldSection in codec-bhttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/bhttp/BinaryHttpParser.java loops while fieldSectionLength is nonzero and relies on disabled-by-default assertions to require BinaryHttpParser.readFieldLine to return a value and consume bytes. A corrupt field line can consume more bytes than its understated declared section length and drive the counter negative, or a truncated field line can return without consuming data and leave the parser in the same state. An unauthenticated OHTTP peer can encrypt such Binary HTTP content under the gateway public configuration, reach OHttpRequestResponseContext.ContentDecoder.decodeChunk, and permanently pin a Netty event-loop thread at full CPU before application business logic. Multiple requests can exhaust the event-loop group and deny service until restart. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser.readFieldLine in codec-bhttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/bhttp/BinaryHttpParser.java treats a complete field line that ends exactly at a known field-section boundary as incomplete and returns without consuming bytes. BinaryHttpParser.readFieldSection then leaves fieldSectionLength unchanged and repeats the loop because its forward-progress checks are Java assertions, which are normally disabled in production. A remote peer that sends a known-length Binary HTTP header or trailer section ending at that boundary can make the parser spin indefinitely and pin the Netty event-loop or worker thread responsible for the channel. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser does not enforce limits on encoded variable-length fields controlled by a remote peer. A remote peer can cause the decoder to buffer data indefinitely until memory is exhausted, causing denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser in codec-bhttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/bhttp/BinaryHttpParser.java accumulates attacker-controlled Binary HTTP variable-length integers into the int offset sumBytes. BinaryHttpParser.readRequestHead, BinaryHttpParser.readFieldLine, and BinaryHttpParser.getIndeterminateLength can narrow long lengths into that offset, causing integer wraparound before buffer indices are calculated. A remote peer that supplies a valid large encoded length to BinaryHttpParser or BinaryHttpDecoder can trigger an unchecked bounds exception from a small malformed message, fail or close the channel, and repeatedly cause denial of service. Java and Netty bounds checks prevent memory corruption, and no information disclosure was observed. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BoringSSLAsymmetricCipherKeyPair.toString in codec-ohttp-hpke-classes-boringssl/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/hpke/boringssl/BoringSSLAsymmetricCipherKeyPair.java includes its private parameter, BoringSSLAsymmetricKeyParameter.toString in codec-ohttp-hpke-classes-boringssl/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/hpke/boringssl/BoringSSLAsymmetricKeyParameter.java renders the complete private-key byte array when isPrivate is true, and BoringSSL.EVP_HPKE_KEY_init_or_throw in codec-ohttp-hpke-classes-boringssl/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/hpke/boringssl/BoringSSL.java includes rejected privateKeyBytes in an exception message. Applications that log affected key-pair objects or initialization exceptions can persist complete HPKE private key material in logs or telemetry. Anyone who can read those records can recover the key and may compromise OHTTP message confidentiality or authenticity expectations while the key remains usable. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.
Greenbone gvmd before 26.43.0 does not restrict certificate creation. Even the Observer role, documented to be read-only, can execute create_tls_certificate.

In Dolibarr before 24.0.3, /api/index.php/eventattendees discloses attendee and project data regardless of the caller's permissions. Only 22.0.0 and later (where api_eventattendees.class.php exists) are affected. A remote authenticated user can obtain column values one character at a time.

In Dolibarr before 24.0.3, dolForgeSQLCriteriaCallback() in htdocs/core/lib/functions.lib.php allows account takeover because it strips only a single table-name prefix from a Universal Search Filter (sqlfilters) operand before checking it against the forbidden-field denylist (pass, pass_crypted, api_key). MariaDB and MySQL accept a two-level qualification such as schema.alias.column, so an operand of the form dolibarr.u.pass_crypted survives the check and is emitted into the WHERE clause. A remote authenticated user holding only the holiday read and readall permissions, which confer no user-management or administrative access, can use the resulting boolean oracle at GET /api/index.php/holidays to recover any user's bcrypt password hash and api_key one character at a time, including an administrator's. Because api_key is accepted directly by the REST API as a bearer credential, this yields full administrative control of the application. This bypasses the fix for CVE-2026-89012, which added only a strtolower() call and did not address prefix depth. The same denylist also omits pass_temp, which stores a password in cleartext, as well as national_registration_number, salary, birth, address, personal_mobile and note_private.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. This vulnerability allows an authenticated remote attacker to cause a denial of service by terminating active sessions of arbitrary users. When processing Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) documents that lack a root signature, Keycloak accepts the request as long as any assertion within the document is signed, without verifying its context or placement. An attacker holding a validly signed assertion can embed it into an unsigned logout request for another user, causing Keycloak to accept the forged request and terminate the victim's session.

Key exchange without entity authentication vulnerability in Apache Tomcat allowed an unauthenticated node to join a cluster when the cluster was secured with TLS 1.3 and TLS-PSK. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: 11.0.28-11.0.29, 10.1.62, 9.0.124. Users are recommended to switch to TLS 1.2 and TLS-PSK or upgrade to version 11.0.30, 10.1.63 or 9.0.125 (when released), which fix the issue.

A weakness has been identified in OSGeo shapelib up to 1.6.3. This vulnerability affects the function DBFCloneEmpty of the file dbfopen.c. This manipulation causes null pointer dereference. It is possible to launch the attack on the local host. Patch name: f79050a900d2a05529501b2b714b8f89067db071. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

Use of cache containing sensitive information vulnerability in Apache Tomcat's ExpiresFilter caused by the filter removing cache-control header fields set by the authentication layer. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.0.M1 through 9.0.123. The following versions were EOL at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: from 8.5.0 through 8.5.100, from 7.0.1 through 7.0.109. Older unsupported versions may also be affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.1.62 or 9.0.124, which fix the issue. Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released

Allocation of resources without limits or throttling vulnerability in Apache Tomcat in the CGI Servlet when handling POST bodies can result in a DoS for some inputs. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.0.M1 through 9.0.123. The following versions were EOL at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: from 8.5.0 through 8.5.100, from 7.0.0 through 7.0.109. Other unsupported versions may also be affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.1.62 or 9.0.124, which fix the issue. Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released

Allocation of resources without limits or throttling vulnerability in Apache Tomcat during HTTP upgrade in some circumstances lead to possible DoS. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.41 through 9.0.123. The following versions were EOL at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: from 8.5.61 through 8.5.100. Other unsupported versions may also be affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.1.62 or 9.0.124, which fix the issue. Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released

Execution After Redirect (EAR) vulnerability in Apache Tomcat in RedirectValve affecting flags [F], [G] and [R]. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M18 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.20 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.87 through 9.0.123. The following versions were EOL at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: 8.5.100. Other unsupported versions may also be affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.1.62, 9.0.124, which fixes the issue. Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released

The fix for CVE-2026-25854 was incomplete. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.19 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.53 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.116 through 9.0.123. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.1.62 or 9.0.124, which fix the issue. Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released

Missing release of resource after effective lifetime vulnerability in Apache Tomcat's HTTP/2 initial connection handling leads to DoS. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.20 through 9.0.123. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.1.62 or 9.0.124, which fix the issue. Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released

Missing release of memory after effective lifetime vulnerability in Apache Tomcat via WebSocket. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.22 through 9.0.123 The following versions were EOL at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: from 8.5.0 through 8.5.100, from 7.0.43 through 7.0.109. Other unsupported versions may also be affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.0.62 or 9.0.124, which fix the issue. Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released

Improper cleanup on thrown exception vulnerability in Apache Tomcat meant that an HTTP 200 response was sent rather than an HTTP 500 response after a AuthException was thrown during Jakarta Authentication secureResponse(). This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.0.M1 through 9.0.123. The following versions were EOL at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: from 8.5.0 through 8.5.100. Other unsupported versions may also be affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.0.62 or 9.0.124, which fix the issue. Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released

Etherpad is a real-time collaborative editor. From 1.8.14 until 3.3.3, the pre-authentication /static/* plugin asset handler in src/node/utils/Minify.ts performs a backslash-to-forward-slash conversion after src/node/utils/sanitizePathname.ts has completed its POSIX path checks. On POSIX systems the sanitizer correctly treats backslashes as ordinary filename bytes, but the later conversion turns encoded backslash-separated parent-directory segments into traversal components without revalidation or containment. The expressPreSession registration and the always-present ep_etherpad-lite core pseudo-plugin make this path reachable without credentials, allowing a remote attacker to read any file available to the Etherpad process. Disclosed configuration or environment secrets can expose administrator credentials, after which the administrator plugin installer can provide in-process code execution and full server compromise. This issue is fixed in version 3.3.3.

Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in Apache Tomcat could occur during a request dispatch if the request depended on a security-role-ref provided by the dispatch target. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.0.M1 through 9.0.123. The following versions were EOL at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: from 8.5.0 through 8.5.100, from 7.0.0 through 7.0.109. Other unsupported versions may also be affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.1.62 or 9.0.124, which fixes the issue. Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released
IBM watsonx.data 2.4.0 through 2.4.0 patch 8 could allow a remote authenticated attacker to conduct a server-side request forgery due to a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability.
IBM watsonx.data 2.4.0 through 2.4.0 patch 8 could allow a remote authenticated attacker to cause a denial of service due to client-side enforcement of business rules.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to SQL injection in the edge-controller component. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability to access or modify sensitive database information.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to improper TLS certificate validation in the GDP Terraform provider, allowing a network attacker with a man-in-the-middle position to intercept sensitive credentials transmitted to the Guardium appliance.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to path traversal in the datasource functionality. An authenticated attacker could exploit this vulnerability to delete arbitrary files on the appliance.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to insecure deserialization in the SharePoint Tap MulticastTransceiver component. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code on the affected system.
IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 could allow a remote attacker to inject forged audit records due to improper output neutralization for logs.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to local privilege escalation via the SUID-root podman_wrapper binary on the Collector appliance. A local attacker with low-privileged access to the Collector can exploit insufficient argument validation in the SUID binary to execute arbitrary commands as root, resulting in full compromise of the Collector appliance.
IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 could allow a remote attacker to obtain sensitive information or cause a denial of service due to an out-of-bounds heap read.

On Intel-based macOS systems, the Okta Device Access (ODA) component of Okta Verify for macOS configures a LaunchDaemon service whose program path resolves via a symbolic link in /usr/local/bin. In environments where non-standard directory permissions grant local non-root users write access to this path, the symbolic link target can be modified, causing the LaunchDaemon to execute the replacement binary upon service restart.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to a stack-based buffer overflow when processing a specially crafted PROXY protocol v1 header. A remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability to cause a denial of service or potentially execute arbitrary code.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to missing authentication in the SharePoint S-TAP RelayService, allowing an unauthenticated network attacker to inject forged audit events and access the active monitoring policy.
IBM watsonx.data 2.4.0 through 2.4.0 patch 8 could allow a local attacker to obtain sensitive credentials due to the use of a hard-coded cryptographic key.

baserCMS is a website development framework. Prior to 5.3.0, getAuthenticationService permits an Api/Admin session authentication fallback based on the Referer header, although operator accounts have an Admin auth prefix and cannot obtain an Api/Admin JWT. An authenticated operator can therefore access /baser/api/admin/ endpoints whose permission.php entries have auth => true, including /baser/api/admin/baser-core/site_configs/view.json, even when the corresponding administrative functionality is restricted. This can disclose administrator-restricted configuration information. This issue is fixed in 5.3.0.

baserCMS is a website development framework. From 5.2.3 until 5.3.0, BcThemeFileService::getFullpath() in plugins/bc-theme-file/src/Service/BcThemeFileService.php skips its path containment check when realpath() fails for a nonexistent theme subdirectory selected by the type parameter. An authenticated administrator can supply a traversal path through the theme-file API to access locations outside the theme directory. The bypass of the CVE-2026-30940 fix can permit file writes, overwrites or deletion within the PHP process permissions and, where executable PHP can be written, remote code execution. This issue is fixed in 5.3.0.

Reposilite is lightweight and easy-to-use repository management software dedicated to Maven-based artifacts in the JVM ecosystem. From 3.5.16 until 3.6.0, as stated by the advisory, the Maven directory-index page interpolates the request URI without HTML escaping in its title, heading, base URL, and parent-directory link. The advisory says the content-embedded ctx.uri() is percent-encoded, preventing tag injection, but that a single quote passes through and breaks the quoted Parent-Directory link; it also says Location.of strips single quotes, so the reachability of the described quote-based trigger remains unresolved. The listing shares the Admin UI origin and does not set the sandbox Content-Security-Policy used for artifact and Javadoc responses, so the reported script execution could access a user's local-storage token. A manager token could enable full instance compromise. The advisory reports version 3.6.0 as fixed.
IBM API Connect 10.0.8.0 through 10.0.8.13 could allow a remote authenticated attacker to delete API keys belonging to other users due to improper authorization checks.
IBM watsonx.data 2.4.0 through 2.4.0 patch 8 could allow a remote attacker to obtain sensitive information due to improper access control.
IBM watsonx.data 2.4.0 through 2.4.0 patch 8 could allow unauthorized network access due to insufficient network segmentation controls.
IBM watsonx.data 2.4.0 through 2.4.0 patch 8 does not invalidate session after a logout which could allow an authenticated user to impersonate another user on the system.

A vulnerability was determined in smartalock wireguard-lwip up to cfba91666590e86bd67842c71cedf9a423be823a. Impacted is the function mul of the file src/crypto/refc/x25519.c of the component X25519 Ladder. Executing a manipulation can lead to out-of-bounds write. The attack can be executed remotely. This product implements a rolling release for ongoing delivery, which means version information for affected or updated releases is unavailable. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

Insufficient verification of data authenticity in the decryption component of Amazon S3 Encryption Client for PHP in AWS SDK for PHP before 3.383.1 might allow an authenticated remote user to forge ciphertext that decrypts to arbitrary plaintext via manipulation of the GCM authentication tag length metadata. To remediate this issue, users should upgrade to AWS SDK for PHP version 3.383.1 or later.

In the Auth0 Authorization Extension, request authentication handling can process claims from query parameters independently of header validation. Under specific preconditions, this may allow an authenticated tenant user to issue requests to the extension's administrative endpoints. Also, input handling during rule generation may permit modification of the tenant login rule published by the extension.

In the Okta .NET SDK Abstractions library, outbound HTTP requests are not restricted to the configured Okta organization domain when processing certain URL formats. If a URL parameter is modified to specify an external host, the library may transmit the configured SSWS API token to that unintended destination.

The Okta Swift Management SDK does not percent-encode forward slash (/) characters during path parameter interpolation. If an application supplies input containing relative path sequences (e.g., ../) to an SDK method, standard URL normalization may direct the outbound request to an alternative Okta Management API endpoint.

The Okta .NET SDK Abstractions library improperly synchronizes authentication credentials set on a shared HTTP client during request execution. When concurrent requests are dispatched for different principals, one principal's credential may be transmitted on an outbound request intended for another principal, which can result in credential exposure and lead to unauthorized actions performed as the affected principal at the Okta Management API.

The Okta .NET SDK Abstractions library systematically writes per-request authentication credentials to a shared HTTP client instance, rather than being isolated to individual outbound request objects. When using scoped child clients, a subsequent scoped request can overwrite the shared client configuration. Because the original parent client credential has not been restored, subsequent outbound requests may be transmitted using the newly written credential, which can result in subsequent actions being executed under the context of an incorrect security principal in the Okta Management API and improper attribution in audit logs.

Collabora Online is a collaborative online office suite based on LibreOffice technology. Prior to 24.04.19.3, 25.04.13.3, and 26.04.3.3, the RouteToken query parameter is reflected into the unauthenticated admin-console page without HTML encoding. The admin-console page is served without authentication. A victim must load a crafted URL, and token exposure requires the victim to be an administrator already signed in to the console; the reflected value can run script in the Collabora Online origin and expose the console authentication token. This issue is fixed in versions 24.04.19.3, 25.04.13.3, and 26.04.3.3.

The Okta Client SDK for Python (okta-client-python) includes client authentication values (client_secret or JWT assertions) as query parameters in the front-channel authorization URL when executing the authorization code flow without Pushed Authorization Requests (PAR). When PAR is disabled, unsupported by the authorization server, or fails, the SDK falls back to standard authorization URL construction, transmitting these parameters via user-agent requests.

Okta Privileged Access (OPA) Gateway includes a version of the FreeRDP library affected by memory management issues in its smartcard redirection handling. When an RDP session is established meeting specific session criteria, command execution within the context of the local Gateway service account may be allowed.

The MongoDB Java Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

The MongoDB Java driver applies its DNS seedlist domain restriction to a record value that is later re-interpreted differently when the connection target is parsed, so the name that is checked and the name that is used can differ. An unauthenticated party who can set or forge the DNS service record for the seed domain in a connection string can cause the driver to direct its session to an unrelated host and to complete certificate verification against that host instead. This may result in unintended disclosure of application data and of configured database credentials, and in unintended content being returned to the application as query results.

A component of the MongoDB Java Driver that processes connection configuration places credential values taken from that configuration into generated text and error output without replacing them with a placeholder, unlike other parts of the driver. A party able to read output produced by an application that embeds the driver may obtain database or proxy credentials in clear text.

CKAN is an open-source data management system for data hubs and data portals. Prior to 2.10.11 and 2.11.6, the web user registration flow authenticates a newly registered account without first regenerating the session identifier when server-side session storage is configured. An attacker who can set a session cookie in a victim's browser or obtain the victim's current valid session identifier can reuse that identifier after the victim registers, gaining access to the new account. CKAN uses cookie-based sessions by default, and web registration is disabled by default through ckan.auth.create_user_via_web. This issue is fixed in CKAN 2.10.11, 2.11.6, and 2.12.0.

ALTCHA is a Go library for creating and verifying ALTCHA challenges. Prior to 2.1.0, parseServerSignature can leave ServerSignatureVerificationData.Extra uninitialized when url.ParseQuery returns partial values and an error for a malformed percent escape in VerificationData. A later write of an unknown parsed key to the nil map panics before VerifyServerSignature or VerifyServerSignatureSafe completes signature verification, so an unauthenticated client can abort a request. Standard net/http recovers the request goroutine, while application goroutines or frameworks without recovery can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 2.1.0.

Aether Project AMF supports termination of NAS signalling, NAS ciphering & integrity protection, registration management, connection management, mobility management, access authentication and authorization, security context management. Prior to 3.1.6, a malformed NGAP PathSwitchRequest can contain a UESecurityCapabilities information element whose extensible APER bit-string representation has no bytes even though decoding reports no error. In ngap/handler.go, HandlePathSwitchRequest checks only whether the element is present before six index-zero reads of its encryption and integrity algorithm fields, causing an unrecovered panic in the NGAP receive goroutine and terminating the AMF. The described attacker is a rogue or compromised gNB on the N2 interface and additionally needs a registered UE's AMF-UE-NGAP-ID; a bare over-the-air UE cannot trigger the issue. This issue is fixed in version 3.1.6.

Connaisseur is an admission controller that integrates container image signature verification into a Kubernetes cluster. Prior to 3.11.1, the Cosign validator counts valid signature layers rather than distinct trust roots for trustRoot: "*" policies using an explicit threshold or an implicit require-all policy. An attacker who controls one configured trust root's signing key and can attach multiple signatures to an image can satisfy a threshold intended to require multiple independent roots, causing admission without the intended signer quorum. Policies using a single trust root or the required option are not affected. This issue is fixed in 3.11.1.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could determine whether a username exists through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API or Splunk Web and lock out existing user accounts through repeated login attempts. The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise returns different login failure responses for locked existing user accounts and nonexistent usernames.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.16, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could cause scheduled metric alert searches to run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands and access credentials stored in cleartext. This requires at least one non-internal metric index on the instance. The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not fully validate metric alert filter input before using it in a scheduled search.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could store attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) in a shared data model. The vulnerability is possible because the Data Model Editor does not properly neutralize data model field names when it builds a preview search. The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the affected user by tricking them into initiating a request within their browser. The attacker should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will. For more information see Add a regular expression field (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/manage-knowledge-objects/knowledge-management-manual/10.4/define-data-model-dataset-fields/add-a-regular-expression-field), Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities), and About the search language (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/search/search-manual/10.4/search-overview/about-the-search-language) in the Splunk documentation.
